To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

people consistently consume significantly more food and non alcoholic drinks from larger sized portions, individual units, packages and tablewares, but there is currently no evidence to suggest this is the case for cigarettes.

exposure to larger sized portions, individual units or tableware consistently increases the amount of food and non alcoholic beverages people select and consume, and that this effect appears to be greater for larger than smaller sized portions, individual packages or tableware.
people consistently consume and select more food and drink from larger sized portions and packages and from shorter, wider tableware.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a potentially important public health target, but the current evidence base is limited in size, methodological quality and scope, and is insufficient to support strong conclusions.
the effects of exposure to varying sizes and sets of physical dimensions on unregulated selection and consumption of products.
the effects of exposure to different sized portions, packages and items of tableware on selection and consumption of unregulated food, alcohol and/or tobacco.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the current evidence is insufficient to draw conclusions about the effects of interventions to manipulate food, tobacco or alcohol product sizes on unregulated selection and consumption in adults or children, or about the extent to which effects might be modified by study design, intervention or participant features.

the effects of exposure to different sizes and shapes of portions, packages and individual units of food and non alcoholic beverages, and of different shaped tableware on food and non alcoholic beverage consumption and selection, are likely to be small to moderate in size and are more likely to be sustained among adults than among children, but are uncertain for alcohol and tobacco products.
the effects of portion size, package size and tableware size on unregulated selection and consumption of foods, alcohol and tobacco in adults and children remain uncertain.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

reducing portion sizes, packages, units and tableware sizes and shapes can help to reduce consumption of food and non alcoholic beverages, but that the evidence for effects on consumption of cigarettes and alcoholic drinks remains uncertain.

, in the absence of other changes in people's food environments, reducing exposure to larger sized portions, individual units or tableware could contribute to reducing the quantities of food and drink people consume.
, in the short term, people consistently consume more when offered larger sized food portions or tableware.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the effects of exposure to different sizes and shapes of products and tableware on consumption and selection of food, alcohol, and tobacco are small to large in magnitude, but that the overall quality of the evidence base is low to moderate, with the exception of the effects of portion and tableware size on the consumption of food, which is rated as moderate.

, if sustained changes to portion, package and tableware size can be achieved across the diet, this could contribute to meaningful reductions to average daily energy consumed by UK adults and children.

the size and shape of food and drinks can have a meaningful influence on the amount of food and drinks that people select and consume, and that this effect may be more pronounced for larger than smaller sizes.
